name: Bot protection
stops: Form spam and bot signups
oneLiner: Stop scripts from filling in your signup, login and contact forms by checking that a person is there.
explain: Bot protection adds checks that scripts find hard to pass, such as a CAPTCHA or Cloudflare Turnstile widget, plus hidden honeypot fields that people never fill in. It stops spam signups, fake comments and automated login attempts. It is not a password defense, since determined attackers can use solving services, so pair it with rate limits and strong login checks.
youCalledIt: stop bots signing up on my site
stop spam from my contact form
stop robots filling in my forms

parts.name: Challenge
parts.desc: The widget or check the visitor must pass, such as Turnstile or a CAPTCHA.

parts.name: Server check
parts.desc: Your server asks the provider if the token is valid before it trusts the form.

parts.name: Honeypot
parts.desc: A hidden field real users leave empty. Bots that fill it in get rejected.

parts.name: Failure rule
parts.desc: What happens when the check fails or the provider is unreachable.

prompt: Find every public form that creates an account, logs in, sends an email or writes data, such as signup, login, password reset and contact forms. Add a bot check to each one, such as Cloudflare Turnstile, and verify its token on the server with the provider's secret key before acting on the submission. Add a hidden honeypot field to forms that do not get a widget, and reject any submission where it is filled in. Keep secret keys on the server only and do not remove other checks. List each protected form and what happens when its check fails.
verify: Submit a signup form with the widget token removed. The server should refuse the request.
Fill in the honeypot field by hand and submit. The request should be rejected.
Submit the form normally as a person. It should succeed.
Open your provider dashboard and confirm solved and rejected challenges show up.

inCode.code:
const r = await fetch('https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/siteverify', { method: 'POST', body: new URLSearchParams({ secret: process.env.TURNSTILE_SECRET, response: req.body['cf-turnstile-response'], remoteip: req.ip }) })
const { success } = await r.json()
inCode.note: Server-side check. Keep the secret key out of browser code.

inCode.code:
const form = await req.formData()
if (form.get('website')) return new Response('Rejected', { status: 400 })
inCode.note: The website field is hidden with CSS and left empty by real users.
The site key is public. The secret key is only used on the server.

name: Spend caps and billing alerts
stops: Surprise bills from bots, loops and bugs
oneLiner: Set hard monthly limits and alerts on cloud and AI accounts, so one bot or bug cannot run up a huge bill.
explain: A spend cap is a hard monthly limit on what a cloud, hosting or AI API account can charge, and a billing alert warns you as spending climbs. They stop a bot, a looping script or a leaked key from running up a large bill before anyone notices. This does not stop an attack, it only limits the damage, so keep rate limits and key protection in place too.
youCalledIt: my api bill went up overnight
stop a huge surprise cloud bill
set a maximum spend on my account
get alerts when my usage spikes
a bot ran up my api costs

parts.name: Hard limit
parts.desc: A monthly ceiling the provider enforces, if it offers one.

parts.name: Budget alert
parts.desc: An email or chat message at 50, 80 and 100 percent of budget.

parts.name: Separate keys
parts.desc: One API key per app or service, so one leak can be revoked alone.

parts.name: Kill switch
parts.desc: A quick way to disable a key or service when usage spikes.

prompt: List every paid external service your app calls, such as LLM providers, email, SMS, maps and cloud compute, and where each one's billing is set up. Set a monthly hard spend limit on each account or project where the provider offers one, plus budget alerts at 50, 80 and 100 percent. Give each service its own API key so you can revoke one without breaking the rest. Make sure the app handles a rejected call from a limit without crashing, and do not remove or lower any existing limit to get a test to pass. List each provider, the limit set, and where alerts go.
verify: In each provider dashboard, confirm a monthly limit or spend cap is set to the amount you chose.
Confirm a budget alert exists and that its email or chat destination receives a test message.
Use a test key with a very low limit and make calls until the provider refuses. Confirm your app shows a friendly error and does not crash.
Check each billing page weekly for the first month for unusual spikes.

inCode.code: const reply = await openai.chat.completions.create({ model, messages, max_completion_tokens: 500 })
inCode.note: Caps output tokens per call. It does not cap your total monthly spend.
max_tokens is deprecated, so use max_completion_tokens.

inCode.code: const reply = await openai.chat.completions.create({ model, messages, max_completion_tokens: 300 })
inCode.note: Set the same cap on every route that calls a paid model.

name: GraphQL hardening
stops: Oversized nested queries and schema snooping
oneLiner: Stop clients sending huge, deeply nested GraphQL queries, and hide your full schema in production.
explain: GraphQL lets one request ask for deeply nested or very expensive data, so a single query can overload your server. Hardening adds limits on query depth and cost, turns off introspection in production so nobody can download your full schema, and can allow only pre-approved queries. This does not check who may see the data, so you still need permission checks on each field and object.
youCalledIt: my graphql api got slow from one request
stop people querying my whole schema
limit how deep graphql queries can go
someone sent a giant graphql query

parts.name: Depth limit
parts.desc: Rejects queries nested more levels deep than you allow.

parts.name: Cost limit
parts.desc: Scores each field and rejects queries above a total budget.

parts.name: Introspection off
parts.desc: Stops clients downloading the full schema in production.

parts.name: Persisted queries
parts.desc: Runs only queries your build registered ahead of time, by ID.

prompt: Find your GraphQL endpoint and its server library, and list the queries your frontend actually sends. Set a maximum query depth and a cost or complexity limit that your real queries fit under, and reject anything above it with a clear error. Turn off schema introspection in production, and where your stack allows, accept only persisted queries. Do not break development tools or the frontend, and do not treat these limits as a replacement for field-level permission checks. List the limits you set and the settings you changed.
verify: Send a query nested deeper than your limit. The server should refuse it without running it.
Send an introspection query such as { __schema { types { name } } } to production. It should return an error.
Load your normal pages. Every real query should still work.
If you use persisted queries, send an unregistered query and confirm it is rejected.

inCode.code:
import depthLimit from 'graphql-depth-limit'
const server = new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers, validationRules: [depthLimit(7)], introspection: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' })
inCode.note: graphql-depth-limit is a community package. Introspection is set explicitly here.

inCode.code:
# In your schema class (class MySchema < GraphQL::Schema)
max_depth 15
max_complexity 300
inCode.note: Counts introspection fields by default, so keep max_depth above 13.
Import graphql.analysis.MaxQueryDepthInstrumentation. Aborts deeper queries.

name: Security logging
stops: Attacks you cannot see
oneLiner: Record logins, failed logins and denied access so you can spot attacks, without logging passwords or tokens.
explain: Security logging writes a record of important events, such as logins, failed logins, password changes and permission denials, with who, what, when and from where. You need these records to notice an attack and to find out what happened afterward. This does not replace monitoring or a full audit trail, and logs must never contain passwords, session tokens or card numbers.
youCalledIt: how do i know if someone hacked my app
see who tried to log in
track suspicious activity on my site

parts.name: Event list
parts.desc: The events you record: logins, failures, lockouts, password changes, access denied.

parts.name: Context
parts.desc: Who, when, which IP address and which request ID for each event.

parts.name: Redaction
parts.desc: Strips passwords, tokens, cookies and card numbers before anything is written.

parts.name: Storage
parts.desc: Where logs go, who can read them, and how long they are kept.

prompt: Find your login, logout, signup, password change, token issue and permission check code. Add structured log entries for successful and failed logins, lockouts, password and role changes, and every 401 and 403 response, each with the user ID or attempted username, IP address, timestamp and request ID. Make sure no password, session token, API key, reset link or card number is ever logged, including in request dumps and error objects. Send logs somewhere searchable that only admins can read, and do not change the business logic. List each event you now log and the fields it contains.
verify: Attempt a login with a wrong password. The log should show a failure with the username and IP address, but not the password.
Request another user's record. Confirm a 403 event appears in the log.
Search the logs for your test password and a real session token. Both searches should return nothing.
Confirm each log line has a timestamp and request ID so you can follow one request across lines.

inCode.code:
const logger = pino({ redact: ['req.headers.authorization', 'req.headers.cookie', 'req.body.password'] })
logger.warn({ event: 'login_failed', username, ip: req.ip }, 'login failed')
inCode.note: redact removes the listed paths from every log line before it is written.
Import receiver, user_login_failed and a logger. Django strips the password.
In config/initializers/filter_parameter_logging.rb. Masks these params in logs.

name: Audit trail
stops: Hidden changes and no record of who did what
oneLiner: Record who changed what and when, in a log the app can add to but never edit or erase.
explain: An audit trail records each important change, such as a role change, a deleted order or a refund, with who made it, when, and the old and new values. Make it append-only, so an attacker or a bug cannot quietly rewrite the history. This does not replace security logging, which watches for attacks. An audit trail answers who changed business data and when.
youCalledIt: keep a history of edits in my app

parts.name: Actor
parts.desc: Who did it: a user ID, an admin ID or a system job.

parts.name: Action and target
parts.desc: What changed and which record it touched.

parts.name: Before and after
parts.desc: The old and new values, with secrets removed.

parts.name: Append-only store
parts.desc: A table or log the app can insert into but not update or delete from.

prompt: Find where users change important data, such as roles, permissions, prices, payments, refunds, deletions and account settings. Add an audit record for each change with the actor ID, action, target type and ID, timestamp, and old and new values with secrets removed. Store these in a separate table or log that the application's database user can insert into but not update or delete from. Do not change how the original data is saved, and do not store passwords or tokens in records. List each audited action and where its records live.
verify: As an admin, change a user's role. Confirm one audit row appears with your ID, the old role and the new role.
Using the app's database user, try to update or delete an audit row. It should fail with a permission error.
Search the audit table for password and token values. Nothing should match.
Trigger a change that fails validation. Confirm no audit row is written for it.

inCode.code:
await prisma.$transaction([prisma.user.update({ where: { id }, data: { role } }),
  prisma.auditLog.create({ data: { actorId, action: 'role.change', targetId: id, before, after } })])
inCode.note: Both writes commit or neither does. auditLog is your own model name.

inCode.code: REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON audit_log FROM anon, authenticated;
inCode.note: Run in the SQL editor. Pair with RLS and check which roles your app uses.
paper_trail stores each change in a versions table. Lock that table down.

name: Safe error messages
stops: Information leaks through error details
oneLiner: Show users a short generic error, and keep stack traces and database details in your server logs only.
explain: When something breaks, error responses should show a short generic message and a reference ID, not stack traces, SQL queries, file paths or library versions. Those details help attackers map your app. The full error still goes to your server logs, so your team can debug it. This does not mean hiding every error: users still need clear messages for input problems, such as 'email is required'.
youCalledIt: stop showing stack trace on my site
my error page shows database info
generic error page for my app

parts.name: Generic message
parts.desc: A short plain message for users, such as 'Something went wrong.'

parts.name: Reference ID
parts.desc: A random ID shown to the user and written to the log, so support can match them.

parts.name: Full server log
parts.desc: Stack trace, query and request details, written only to logs.

parts.name: Debug mode off
parts.desc: Framework debug pages disabled in production.

prompt: Find every error handler, global exception filter and debug setting in the app. Make sure production responses return a generic message and a request ID, never stack traces, SQL text, file paths, environment values or library versions. Log the full error on the server with the same request ID. Keep helpful messages for validation errors, such as which field is missing, since users need those. Do not remove logging or change how errors are caught. List the handlers you changed and the production settings you turned off.
verify: Send a request that causes a server error. The response should be generic, with no stack trace or file path.
Search the response body for file paths like /src/ and SQL words like SELECT. Neither should appear.
Copy the request ID from the response and find the same ID in your server log next to the full error.
Visit a path that does not exist and confirm no framework debug page appears.

inCode.note: Register after all routes. Four arguments make Express treat it as an error handler.
Django shows tracebacks only when DEBUG is True.
In config/environments/production.rb. Confirm nothing overrides it.

name: Monitoring and alerting
stops: Attacks and outages nobody notices
oneLiner: Get an alert when your site goes down, or when errors, failed logins or 403s suddenly spike.
explain: Uptime monitoring checks from outside that your site responds, and alerting tells you when a number jumps, such as a burst of 401 or 403 responses or a wave of 500 errors. Those spikes often mean an attack, a bad deploy or a broken key. This does not replace logging: an alert only says something is wrong, so you still need logs to find out what happened.
youCalledIt: tell me when my site goes down
get an email if my app is under attack
alert me when there are lots of errors
know when someone hammers my login

parts.name: Uptime check
parts.desc: An outside service that requests a URL every minute or so.

parts.name: Baseline
parts.desc: The normal rate of errors, logins and 403s to compare against.

parts.name: Spike rule
parts.desc: Alerts when a count stays well above baseline for a few minutes.

parts.name: Destination
parts.desc: Where alerts go, such as email or chat, with a named owner.

prompt: Add an external uptime check for your main URL and a health endpoint, and send alerts to a place someone reads. Count 401, 403 and 500 responses per minute from your logs or error tracker, and create an alert that fires when a count rises well above normal for several minutes. Start with thresholds you can tune, and do not page on every single error. Include the route and count in each alert so the person on duty knows where to look. List each check and alert, its threshold and its destination.
verify: Point the uptime check at a broken URL for a few minutes. Confirm you get an alert within the expected time.
Send a burst of failed logins to a staging copy. Confirm the 401 spike alert fires.
Confirm the alert text includes the route and the count.
Restore the URL and check that a recovery message arrives.

inCode.note: Point your uptime checker here. Return nothing secret.
Included by default in recent Rails apps. Check the route exists.
In application.properties. Expose only health, not every actuator endpoint.

name: Security.txt file
stops: Security bug reports with nowhere to go
oneLiner: A small text file at /.well-known/security.txt that tells security researchers how to report a bug to you.
explain: A security.txt file is a plain text file at /.well-known/security.txt, defined by RFC 9116, that lists how to contact your security team and when the file expires. Researchers who find a bug can use it instead of guessing where to send a report. This does not offer a bug bounty, reward or permission to test, so state your rules in the Policy line if you want them.
youCalledIt: how do people report security bugs to me
where to send a security report
let hackers report bugs to me

parts.name: Contact
parts.desc: Required. A mailto: or https: address where reports go.

parts.name: Expires
parts.desc: Required. A date after which the file is stale, in ISO 8601 format.

parts.name: Policy
parts.desc: Optional link to your disclosure rules.

parts.name: Location
parts.desc: Served at /.well-known/security.txt over HTTPS.

prompt: Create a security.txt file with a Contact address that a person reads, an Expires date within the next year, and a Policy URL if you have one. Serve it as plain text at https://yourdomain.com/.well-known/security.txt with no redirect and no login. Update the Expires date before it passes, and do not put secrets or internal details in the file. Add a link to it from your site footer or security page if you have one. List the file contents, where it is served, and the Expires date you chose.
verify: Open https://yourdomain.com/.well-known/security.txt in a browser. You should see plain text, not an error page.
Check that the Expires date is in the future and written in ISO 8601 with a timezone, such as 2027-12-31T23:59:59.000Z.
Compare the file with the rules and examples at securitytxt.org.
Send a test email to the Contact address and confirm it arrives.

inCode.note: Replace the example address and date. Serve over HTTPS.
Adjust the file path. alias maps this exact URL to the file.
